analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to publicly disclose their political spending each year.
analysis.headline: The bill to require public companies to disclose their political spending was introduced with one cosponsor, referred to the Financial Services Committee, and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended securities law to require publicly traded companies to report each year what they spend on politics — including independent election spending, political ads, and payments to trade associations and tax-exempt groups that can be passed along for political use — and to publish that summary on a public website. It also directed the SEC to write the detailed rules within 90 days of enactment. The goal was to let shareholders and voters trace corporate money into elections, including money routed through groups that keep donors hidden. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters gain the ability to see which companies are bankrolling candidates and political ads, including money funneled through trade associations and 501(c) groups where the original funder is usually hidden. Shareholders also gain, since they currently cannot see how the companies they own are spending money on politics. Candidates and advocacy groups that disclose their own funding would compete on a more level field with hidden corporate money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and shareholders of public companies

how_it_helps.text: Requires every public company that files an annual report to disclose a summary of its political spending for the prior year and publish it on a website open to shareholders and the public, so voters and investors can trace corporate money in elections.

Covers not just direct election spending and political ads but also dues and payments to trade associations and 501(c) organizations when those payments could be used or transferred for political purposes — closing the most common route corporations use to spend on politics without being identified.

Directs the SEC to issue implementing regulations within 90 days of enactment, using an existing disclosure system companies already comply with, so the information would be filed regularly rather than left voluntary.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations and the trade associations and tax-exempt groups that receive corporate dues would bear the cost of tracking, summarizing, and publishing their political spending, and would lose the ability to fund candidates and ads without their names becoming public.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public corporations and their trade associations

drawbacks.text: Public companies would face real compliance costs to track political spending across subsidiaries, trade associations, and 501(c) groups and produce annual summaries — the kind of expense small public companies feel more than giants.

Because the bill requires only a 'summary' of expenditures, its rules could have been written to allow companies to lump spending into broad categories, limiting how useful the disclosure actually is to voters.

Supporters would acknowledge that naming corporate funders invites public pressure and boycotts of companies over their political giving, and that the bill does nothing about the underlying rules — written by the FEC and courts — that allow unlimited political spending in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — letting voters and shareholders see who is funding political campaigns — outweighs the compliance cost, which falls on companies that already file detailed annual reports and could absorb this as one more section. The main weakness is that a 'summary' standard leaves room for rules that produce less detail than a full itemized accounting, and the bill cannot be judged on final design because the SEC rules it called for were never written.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Financial Services Committee, and the committee never held a hearing or a vote on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the Corporate Political Disclosure Act of 2019 on February 7, 2019, with Rep. Zoe Lofgren as its one cosponsor.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, which handles securities law.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded corporations, trade associations, and tax-exempt groups that fund political activity are better off because the bill died: they can keep spending on elections through intermediaries without ever being named.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations that fund politics through hidden channels

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on February 7, 2019.

for.name: Rep. Zoe Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat with no recorded action for the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: House leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with only one cosponsor and no committee action, it was never a candidate for a vote.

against.name: Publicly traded corporations and trade associations
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the bill's inaction; corporate disclosure requirements of this kind have historically drawn organized industry opposition, though no specific opposition from these groups appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two House sponsors, both Democrats, and never advanced far enough for either chamber to record a party-line vote; its fate was a lack of sponsorship and committee inaction rather than an identifiable partisan bloc.

industries.note: The bill would have forced companies to name their political spending — including money sent through trade associations and 501(c) groups — ending the current ability to influence elections without being identified. Its defeat preserves that anonymity.

These groups would have had corporate dues traced to them when passed along for political use, making them far less useful as hiding places for campaign money. The bill's death keeps their role intact.
The industry profits from political spending whose corporate funders are often invisible; without disclosure, that money keeps flowing with no accountability to the voters it targets.
